title: The Happy Prince and Other Tales
description: Five fairy tales by Oscar Wilde about gifts nobody notices: a statue and a swallow give everything to the poor, a nightingale dies for a rose, a giant learns to share his garden.
source_title: The Happy Prince and Other Tales

cover.alt: A cloaked beggar crouching at the gates while the rich make merry in a lit palace beyond
cover.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The statue and the swallow
elements.text: A swallow late for Egypt shelters at the feet of the gilded Happy Prince and is soaked by the statue's tears.

metadata.source_quote: “When I was alive and had a human heart,” answered the statue, “I did not know what tears were

image.alt: Young people lounging in a sunlit palace garden: the Palace of Sans-Souci
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The ruby, the sapphires
elements.text: Night after night the Prince sends the swallow to carry his ruby to a seamstress and his sapphire eyes to a poor playwright and a match-girl.

metadata.source_quote: will you not stay with me for one night, and be my messenger?

image.alt: The loveliest of the Queen's maids of honour, in a pale gown and tall headdress
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: Leaf by leaf
elements.text: Now blind, the Prince has the swallow strip his gold leaf for the poor. Winter comes; the swallow dies at his feet and the lead heart cracks.

metadata.source_quote: “I am covered with fine gold,” said the Prince, “you must take it off, leaf by leaf, and give it to my poor

image.alt: A cloaked beggar crouching at the gates while the rich make merry in a lit palace beyond
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The two most precious things
elements.text: The Mayor melts down the shabby statue. The lead heart will not melt and is thrown on a dust-heap with the dead bird; an angel carries both to God.

metadata.source_quote: “Bring me the two most precious things in the city,” said God to one of His Angels

elements.title: A red rose
elements.text: A Student despairs: the Professor's daughter will dance with him only if he brings a red rose, and there are none in his garden.

image.alt: A young woman in an elegant patterned gown passes by while the Student watches
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The thorn
elements.text: To make a red rose the Nightingale sings all night with her heart against a thorn, and dies. The girl prefers jewels; the Student throws the rose in the gutter.

metadata.source_quote: “Death is a great price to pay for a red rose,” cried the Nightingale

image.alt: A winged figure of Love with a bow, standing barefoot in a rose-coloured haze
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: Trespassers will be prosecuted
elements.text: The Giant comes home, finds children in his garden and walls them out. Spring never comes; the garden stays in winter.

elements.title: The children come back
elements.text: Children creep in through a hole and the trees blossom. The Giant lifts a little boy into a tree and knocks the wall down.

metadata.source_quote: “How selfish I have been!” he said; “now I know why the Spring would not come here.

image.alt: Children climbing a tree white with blossom in the Giant's garden
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The wounds of Love
elements.text: Years later the little boy returns with wounds in his hands and feet and takes the old Giant to his own garden, Paradise.

metadata.source_quote: “Nay!” answered the child; “but these are the wounds of Love.”

image.alt: The little boy in a yellow robe standing among white blossom and cloud
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: Little Hans and the Miller
elements.text: The rich Miller talks beautifully about friendship and takes everything from little Hans, who dies running an errand for him in a storm.

metadata.source_quote: Little Hans had a great many friends, but the most devoted friend of all was big Hugh the Miller.

image.alt: Little Hans in a wide hat, working in his garden among the roses
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: A very remarkable Rocket
elements.text: At a royal wedding a vain rocket cries and talks too much, gets damp, is thrown in a ditch and explodes in the daytime with nobody watching.

metadata.source_quote: “I knew I should create a great sensation,” gasped the Rocket, and he went out.

image.alt: The King in his crown and furs, a courtier bowing low: Let the fireworks begin
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The Happy Prince
elements.text: A gilded statue with sapphire eyes and a lead heart, who as a living prince never knew sorrow and as a statue sees nothing else.

image.alt: Young people lounging in a sunlit palace garden: the Palace of Sans-Souci
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The Swallow
elements.text: A frivolous little bird in love with a reed, who stays one more night, and one more, and gives up Egypt for the Prince.

metadata.source_quote: I am waited for in Egypt

elements.title: The Nightingale
elements.text: A bird who believes love is worth more than life and proves it.

image.alt: A winged figure of Love with a bow, standing barefoot in a rose-coloured haze
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The Student
elements.text: A young man of books who wants a rose to win a dance, and decides afterwards that logic is more useful than love.

image.alt: A young woman in an elegant patterned gown passes by while the Student watches
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The Selfish Giant
elements.text: A giant who walls in his garden after seven years with the Cornish ogre, and learns too late what the wall cost him.

metadata.source_quote: My own garden is my own garden

image.alt: Children climbing a tree white with blossom in the Giant's garden
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The little boy
elements.text: The smallest child in the Giant's garden, too little to reach the tree; he returns years later with the wounds of Love.

image.alt: The little boy in a yellow robe standing among white blossom and cloud
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: Little Hans
elements.text: A kind, poor gardener who believes his rich friend the Miller, whatever it costs him.

image.alt: Little Hans in a wide hat, working in his garden among the roses
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The Remarkable Rocket
elements.text: A firework who thinks the world was made to admire him.

metadata.source_quote: I am a very remarkable Rocket, and come of remarkable parents.

image.alt: The King in his crown and furs, a courtier bowing low: Let the fireworks begin
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The city square
elements.text: A city of rich houses and poor attics, seen from the top of the Prince's column.

image.alt: A cloaked beggar crouching at the gates while the rich make merry in a lit palace beyond
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The Palace of Sans-Souci
elements.text: The palace where the prince lived, where sorrow was not allowed in; its name means "without care".

image.alt: Young people lounging in a sunlit palace garden: the Palace of Sans-Souci
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The Giant's garden
elements.text: A lovely garden with soft grass and twelve peach-trees, locked in winter while the wall stands.

image.alt: Children climbing a tree white with blossom in the Giant's garden
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The King's palace
elements.text: The setting of The Remarkable Rocket, where the Prince marries the Russian Princess who arrived in a sledge drawn by six reindeer.

image.alt: The Russian Princess arriving in a sledge drawn by reindeer, a domed city behind
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: Talking creatures and objects
elements.text: Statues, birds, trees, fireworks and water-rats all speak and judge each other, usually wrongly.

elements.title: Heaven's ledger
elements.text: Earthly authorities judge by appearance and use; God's judgment, in the last lines, reverses theirs.

elements.title: Charity that costs everything
elements.text: The Prince and the swallow give until there is nothing left of either. The gift is real; the reward is not of this world.

metadata.source_quote: There is no Mystery so great as Misery.

image.alt: A cloaked beggar crouching at the gates while the rich make merry in a lit palace beyond
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: Beauty judged by use
elements.text: The town admires the statue while it glitters and melts it the moment it doesn't.

metadata.source_quote: As he is no longer beautiful he is no longer useful

elements.title: Love against Logic
elements.text: The Nightingale gives her life for a rose; the Student cannot see the point of it.

metadata.source_quote: It is not half as useful as Logic

image.alt: A young woman in an elegant patterned gown passes by while the Student watches
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: Words as a lever
elements.text: The Miller's speeches about friendship are how he exploits Hans. Wilde distrusts people who talk well about virtue.

image.alt: Little Hans in a wide hat, working in his garden among the roses
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: The Passion
elements.text: The Giant's last visitor carries the prints of nails in his hands and feet: Wilde's tale closes in the language of the Passion.

image.alt: The little boy in a yellow robe standing among white blossom and cloud
image.credit: Charles Robinson, colour plate for The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1913 edition). Public domain.

elements.title: Sans-Souci
elements.text: Frederick the Great's summer palace at Potsdam, named "without care".
